articles.title: From being fired at her job at 27 to building an $800 million luxury brand: How Tamara Mellon turned a career crisis into a fashion empire
articles.summary: UK News: At 27, Tamara Mellon was at a difficult point in her career. In 1995, she had lost her job at British Vogue, had gone through rehabilitation for drug .
articles.body: At 27, Tamara Mellon was at a difficult point in her career. In 1995, she had lost her job at British Vogue, had gone through rehabilitation for drug use and was living in her parents' basement. A few years later, she would be at the centre of one of the biggest luxury footwear businesses of its time. Mellon went on to co-found Jimmy Choo with London-based shoemaker Jimmy Choo in 1996. The company, which began with a £150,000 investment from her father, grew from a small London operation into an international luxury label. As per the official website of Vogue, in 2011, Jimmy Choo was sold to Labelux for £525.5 million, roughly $800 million at the time. But the business began much more modestly.The shoemaker she knew from VogueMellon had worked as an accessories editor at British Vogue. During those years, she regularly visited Jimmy Choo's workshop in London's East End to have shoes made for fashion shoots. In a 2011 interview with British Vogue, she recalled how she used Choo's work for fashion shoots, saying: "I used to go down and I used to get Jimmy to make things for shoots. I'd go down to his studio in Hackney and I'd say 'OK I want a gladiator sandal with studs, and I want it in metallic silver.'" Choo would make the shoes, she would photograph them and credit him in Vogue. "But that's how his name became known - because I was doing that for five years," she said in the interview.According to her, Choo was a skilled bespoke shoemaker, but his business was small. Mellon saw an opportunity to take his craftsmanship beyond individual clients and build a ready-to-wear luxury footwear company. The idea was that Choo would bring the shoemaking expertise, while Mellon would handle the business. In the same interview, she recalled approaching him: "OK we will be equal partners in this. I will run all the operations." She then went to Italy, found factories and set up the production company. Getting Choo to agree, however, took persistence. According to Mellon, she spent months around his workshop trying to prove that she was serious about building a company with him.Borrowed £150,000 from her fatherMellon's father, entrepreneur Tommy Yeardye, eventually backed the idea with £150,000. Mellon herself has described the money as a loan. In a Forbes interview, she recalled: "I borrowed 150 grand [£150,000, or $230,000] from my father, and everything was set up." The early company was far removed from the polished luxury image Jimmy Choo would later develop. Mellon and the team worked from a basement office. She had little experience running a shoe company, so she had to learn the manufacturing side as she went. In a British Vogue interview, she described doing almost everything herself in the early days: **"When I look back at the early days I was helping customers on the shop floor. I was cleaning the shop floor and then running downstairs to fax orders to the factories in Italy."Mellon understood the power of celebritiesOne of Mellon's biggest business decisions was to put Jimmy Choo shoes directly in front of celebrities. The strategy connected luxury footwear with Hollywood red carpets at a time when celebrity fashion was becoming increasingly influential. Jimmy Choo shoes began appearing with famous actresses and on major award-show red carpets. Mellon later explained that she recognised this shift early. In a 2013 interview with Vogue, she said: "That's why I took the brand to the Oscars, because I saw that early." She described the period as a time when ‘celebrity was exploding’ and magazines were increasingly putting actresses on their covers rather than models. The brand received another major boost from Sex and the City. Carrie Bradshaw's attachment to Jimmy Choo shoes helped introduce the label to viewers far beyond the fashion industry.By the end of 2000, Mellon wrote in her memoir that Jimmy Choo was making about 3 million euros in annual profit, had its own London store and was represented in around 450 other stores, including Harrods and Selfridges.Jimmy Choo eventually became an $800 million businessThe company's growth continued through a series of investment deals. Jimmy Choo was sold to Labelux in 2011 for 525.5 million euros, commonly reported as about $800 million. British Vogue reported that Mellon received an estimated 85 million euros from the sale. Mellon later spoke about what she had learned from building the company. In a Vogue interview, she gave a simple piece of advice: "Keep control of your business."The career setback she later called a wake-up callMellon's difficult period before Jimmy Choo was not something she hid. In interviews around the publication of her memoir ‘In My Shoes,’ she spoke openly about her drug and alcohol problems and her departure from Vogue. In an interview about her life and career, Mellon recalled: "I got fired from Vogue and because I was my drug addiction started getting out of control. I was you know 26, 27 years old and I got fired from Vogue and I got scared." She said she later returned to thank the woman who had fired her, Vogue editor Anna Harvey. "I actually years later I went back and I thanked the woman who fired me. I went back and I actually thanked her because it was the wakeup call I needed and I got scared enough to get sober and change my life."What came after Jimmy Choo?Mellon left Jimmy Choo in 2011 and later launched her fashion label with her name. Looking back at her first company, she has described the early years as a period when she was involved in almost every part of the operation. In a 2011 British Vogue interview, she said: "What excites me most is the thrill of the next project, the next idea."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A 67-year-old Idaho teacher retired and drove across the US to Delaware after her daughter's daycare bill matched the mortgage; she now provides about 30 hours of childcare every week for her granddaughter
articles.summary: US News: A 67-year-old retired schoolteacher from Idaho moved across the US to Delaware after her daughter decided to have a second child despite the high cost.
articles.body: A 67-year-old retired schoolteacher from Idaho moved across the US to Delaware after her daughter decided to have a second child despite the high cost of childcare. Mary Jo Galusha retired from teaching and drove cross-country in her red Volkswagen Beetle to help her daughter, Stacia Bourne, and her family, WTJX NewsFeed reported.Bourne, a University of Delaware psychology professor who lives in Maryland, and her husband had been worried about the cost of raising another child. Their first child, George, was born in 2020 and started daycare at the age of two. "The cost for childcare for him is about the same as our mortgage," Bourne said.The couple had been discussing whether they could afford a second child when Galusha offered to help. She told her daughter that if they decided to have another baby, she would retire and move from Idaho to the East Coast to provide childcare.Several months later, Galusha received the call that Bourne was expecting. "I got a call that Stacia was expecting and that I better start planning on retiring," Galusha recalled with a laugh. She then retired from her job as a schoolteacher, packed her belongings and made the long drive to Delaware.Galusha, who is now the grandmother of five, lives in Newark, Delaware. Her granddaughter Robin was born in late 2024 and spends about 30 hours a week in Galusha's care while her parents work. Galusha has also replaced her Volkswagen Beetle with an SUV so that two car seats can fit more easily in the back row. "It's a joy," Galusha said. "It's like magic to watch them grow up."Rising costs push families to grandparentsGalusha's decision comes as more families in the US are relying on grandparents for childcare. Grandparents have always helped look after grandchildren, but rising childcare costs have made that support more important for families who cannot easily afford daycare.According to Child Care Aware of America, the average annual cost of childcare for children under five in the US was $13,184 in 2025. In some cases, childcare costs can be close to the cost of rent or college tuition.Nicole Jorwic, chief programme officer at Caring Across Generations, said families are turning to older relatives because of gaps in the childcare system."The reality is that because this country hasn't invested in a childcare infrastructure that is flexible and affordable and reliable, grandparents are filling in the gaps that the service system leaves behind," she said.Madonna Harrington Meyer, a Syracuse University sociology professor who studies ageing and grandparenting, said several factors have increased the need for childcare. More households now have both parents working full-time, while the number of single mothers has also increased over the decades.Families raising children with disabilities can face another challenge because they may need childcare providers who can offer specialised care. "All of these things are reasons people turn to grandparents," Harrington Meyer said.Millions of grandparents provide regular careGalusha is one of millions of grandparents who help care for grandchildren. One poll found that nearly half of respondents with grandchildren under 18 looked after them at least once every few months.An AARP report from June found that the main reasons grandparents provide childcare include parents being busy or working and grandparents wanting to spend time with their grandchildren.The median amount of time grandparents spent caring for grandchildren, excluding those who are primary caregivers or provide no care, was 200 hours a year, or about 3.8 hours a week, according to the data.Having grandparents provide childcare can also offer greater flexibility than formal daycare. Harrington Meyer said grandparents may care for children at their own homes or at the children's homes and can adjust arrangements around the family's needs."They are so flexible," Harrington Meyer said. "Unlike a formal daycare situation, often grandparents will come to your house, or they'll alternate between watching the children at their own house and at the grandparent's house."Grandparents can also benefit from spending time with their grandchildren. One study found higher scores on memory and verbal fluency tests among grandparents who provided care.Sacrifice for grandparentsHowever, providing regular childcare can be demanding, particularly for older people who have already raised their own children. It can affect their physical health, social lives and careers. Grandparents who move to be closer to their grandchildren may also leave behind friends and familiar surroundings.Jerry Larkin, 66, a former machinist, moved in with his daughter's family in Tulsa, Oklahoma, during the Covid-19 pandemic to help care for his twin grandsons. One of the children requires additional medical care."Being raised in the '60s, there were a lot of stay-at-home moms and everything, so this wasn't really a thing," Larkin said. "But now that everybody's got to work two jobs, it's become a thing."Yalanda Lattimore, 59, also provides regular care for her one-year-old granddaughter, Mavee. She looks after her for one and a half days each week. Lattimore said the arrangement has reduced the time she can spend on her handmade soap business and media work."I felt like I could make the sacrifice more than they could, and it truly has been a sacrifice," she said. "You just put things on hold, because your priorities are different."Galusha plans to care until kindergartenFor Galusha, her pension from her years as a schoolteacher in Idaho makes it possible to provide unpaid childcare after retirement. Her home in Newark has a bedroom for her grandchildren, a playroom filled with Legos and a crafting area for George.Galusha and Bourne use a shared Google Calendar to organise the children's care. The current plan is for Galusha to look after Robin until she starts kindergarten, although the two review the arrangement every six months.Bourne said having her mother provide the care gives the family a sense of security, but there is little backup if the arrangement changes."I'd much prefer to have my mom take care of Robin, but then you always worry, like if in six months she decides that she wants to move and be near another grandbaby, then we'll have to scramble and figure out something else," Bourne said. Galusha responded from across the table, "No plans for that."For Lattimore, the time spent caring for her granddaughter is also about being present for her family. "What you really want is somebody to say you were there, that you were there for them," she said. "Those are the memories that I want."She said parents should not have to choose between paying for childcare and giving up work. After raising four children herself, she wanted her daughter to have a different experience."When my daughter got ready to start her family, I just didn't want her to go through that," Lattimore said. "I wanted her to have the balance. If work-life balance exists for somebody, I wanted it for my daughter," she added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Two 100-year-old Iowa homes were headed for demolition; after an 18-month rescue, both have been renovated and will now become affordable housing for two refugee families in Davenport
articles.summary: US News: Two century-old homes in Davenport that had once been marked for demolition have gained a new lease on life and are set to become homes for refugee fa.
articles.body: Two century-old homes in Davenport that had once been marked for demolition have gained a new lease on life and are set to become homes for refugee families. Foundation of First Presbyterian Church and Tapestry Farms led an eighteen-month effort to transform these homes.The project was inspired by a concert in March 2025 by the Justice Choir of the Midwest that benefited Tapestry Farms where the need for housing for refugee families was highlighted. The church then cancelled the demolition contract and began working with the organisation to rehabilitate the homes. It will welcome new families into the neighbourhood near First Presbyterian Church in central Davenport. "These houses have already been part of this community for more than 100 years," said Nancy Chapman, a member of First Presbyterian who led the project. "Now they have the opportunity to serve our community in a renewed way. They will be lived in, cared for and filled with the everyday moments that make a house a home.""In a time when our community is struggling with having enough affordable housing, the renovation of these two homes represents one model of how collaboration can turn viable, yet vacant, housing into beautiful homes," added Ann McGlynn, founder and executive director of Tapestry Farms.Over the past 18 months, crews have worked to rehabilitate the two properties and bring them back to life. The $180,000 project required the commitment and collaboration of numerous organisations, funders, contractors and individual donors.McGlynn said the renovation included new flooring, bathrooms and kitchens, along with painting and other improvements. Falcon Home Improvements served as the project's contractor. Director Shawn Manning said crews repaired or replaced furnaces, ductwork, plumbing, electrical systems, roofs, porches and other parts of the properties."There's nothing on these properties that we haven't touched in order to get it ready and safe for a family to come into," Manning said. McGlynn said the homes' original features were worth preserving. "Oh, but they have such good bones," McGlynn said. "You know, there are fireplaces and there are cabinets that are built into the walls and beautiful woodwork and so it was just a matter of uncovering all of that and making it shine again," McGlynn added, saying the homes will provide more than just a place to live. They include backyards where the families can grow gardens and are near a playground, school, bank and other amenities.For project manager Lupe Morales-Salsido, the work carried a personal connection. She said she comes from a large family and that her parents immigrated to the United States. "It just gave me a lot of pride," Morales-Salsido said.The two refugee families are expected to move into the renovated homes in the coming weeks.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Grand jury declines to bring criminal charges in Nolan Wells death
articles.summary: Nolan Wells' family had raised alarm that he ended up dead "after going out on a boat with three young white men".
articles.body:
A grand jury will not bring criminal charges against anyone in the death of a Mississippi teenager, who was found dead two days after a boating trip with friends on 4 July.

Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney hired by the family, had raised concerns that Nolan Wells, a black man, "ended up dead after going out on a boat with three young white men", and that there had been conflicting witness statements.

Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath said the grand jury indicated there was not enough evidence to charge someone with a crime in the death of Wells.

In a statement to US media, Crump said the grand jury result "leaves us with more questions than answers".

"Nolan's family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we," he said.

Police had said Wells accidentally drowned, with his friends saying he chose to stay back on Horn Island after they decided to leave early because of an issue with their boat.

A report from the grand jury posted on the district attorney's social media on Monday found that the "position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr Wells' body is consistent with drowning".

"There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan's death and disappearance were racially motivated," Myers McIlrath said in the video message.

According to the report, 25 grand jurors heard from 43 witnesses, including a forensic pathologist hired by Wells' family to conduct an independent autopsy.

"The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 ... engaged in any criminal conduct related to ​the death of Mr. Wells," the report said.

The report said those who travelled with Wells were fully cooperative and offered GPS devices, surveillance footage, cell phones and other evidence.

It also said it is not unusual for visitors to Horn Island to stay and leave on different boats than they came on on crowded holiday days.

Wells' mother Christine Wonsley was the first to raise the alarm that her son, who played American football at Southwest Mississippi Community College and was described by his coach as a "happy-go-lucky kid", had gone missing after he did not return on the evening of 4 July.

Authorities discovered his body off the coast of the island on 6 July, following a search that included multiple local, state and federal agencies.

articles.title: Tech layoffs 2026: Tracking all the job losses across Apple, Oracle, Uber, TikTok, Meta, Microsoft and others
articles.summary: We're more than half way through the year, and there have already been more than 185,000 layoffs across the tech industry — here's what we know.
articles.body:
We've been inundated with tech layoffs throughout the whole of 2026 — and there's likely more to come. In June, 14,000 job cuts happened at EV automaker Lucid, game developer Bungie, trading platform company Robinhood and others. Microsoft 's latest round of layoffs happened shortly after, affecting 4,800 jobs — mostly across its Xbox gaming division. Following that, companies like Samsung, Zillow and even TikTok joined the club.

According to many reports , the U.S. is at the center of these job cuts. Oracle has had the biggest impact on layoffs this year so far. The annual financial disclosure the company filed on June 23 showed the software giant cut 21,000 jobs over the past year, roughly 13% of its workforce.

"The adoption and deployment of AI technologies across our operations have resulted, and may continue to result, in reductions to our workforce," Oracle said in the filing.

In response to the numerous job cuts, California Governor Gavin Newsom in June unveiled a tool to track AI's impact on the workforce . "As AI advances, we aren't just watching from the sidelines; we're reimagining how we prepare California through strong governance and innovative policy." And recently, more than 4,500 Google workers signed a petition calling for layoff protections as things get worse. Some of the protections they're asking for include buyouts before mandatory layoffs and guaranteed severance.

TrueUp finds that layoffs seem to be moving at a faster rate than last year — over 245,000 workers in tech were let go in 2025, while there have been more than 185,000 layoffs in 2026 so far. Several of the companies below have laid off employees due to increased spending in AI. We'll get into the reasons for the layoffs.

According to a Bloomberg report , Apple has laid off an undisclosed number of employees from Fitness+, the company's exercise subscription service. According to the report, the layoffs affected those who worked in the audio side of the division, which includes features like Time to Walk and Time to Run guided audio workouts. Reportedly, offerings like this will be reduced — but not eliminated completely — from the service.

Oracle employees were impacted by yet another round of layoffs in September. The total number of employees laid off this time around is not currently known. The tech giant reportedly set employees early morning emails on Monday, September 14, letting those affected know it would be their last working day. It's also reported that, with these layoffs, Oracle is looking to offset the amount of money is pouring into AI chips and data centers. Earlier this year, Oracle laid off 21,000 people.

Uber announced it will cut 3,300 jobs, or about 10% of its workforce, in a big restructuring effort. "We are removing layers, simplifying team structures, refining our global location strategy, and focusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in a statement . While the cuts apply to both regular employees and managers, the company stated it will reduce the "number of employees who sit 7+ layers from the CEO" by 20%, and it will cut the number of "micro-teams" by almost 50%. The CEO's memo did not mention AI as catalyst for the layoffs, but it did explain that this restructuring will allow Uber to bring its services to more people, invest in more drivers and merchants and "build the autonomous future."

According to an AppleInsider report , Apple laid off at least 60 people in its Vision Group, which is the team responsible for the Vision Pro VR headset. A Bloomberg report notes that Apple is also laying off roles in its Intelligent Systems Experience group, which is partially responsible for some of the AI systems on Apple devices. Overall, its estimated the layoffs affect more than 200 people.

When it comes to Vision Group and Vision Pro, it's been reported that incoming CEO John Ternus would be putting that product category "on ice," so this seems like the start of that process. The Vision Pro headset came out in 2024 with an eye-watering $3,699 starting price, and it remains to be seen if Apple will be pulling out of the AR/VR category entirely in the future. The Intelligence Systems changes are reportedly tied to changes that are necessary for the technical architecture for Apple's newly AI-infused Siri.

The New York Times reported that TikTok will lay off 250 people and close its Nashville, Tennessee office in October. This location was home to, in part, some of TikTok's content moderation team, although the company has not specified the reason for the layoffs or which teams they primarily affect. "We have decided to close our Nashville office to streamline our operations and better align our teams for long-term growth," a press officer for what is known as the TikTok U.S.D.S. Joint Venture said in a statement to the Times.

Zillow will lay off just over 500 people as it enacts organizational changes across the company. "These are difficult decisions that reflect both the strides we're making in our strategy and the reality of what is required of us to grow at scale," CEO Jeremy Wacksman wrote in a press release . Wacksman didn't go into detail about what organizational changes were made, or which departments are bearing the brunt of the layoffs. "These changes are about ensuring we have a disciplined cost structure and getting more efficient, with the right people in the right positions," he wrote.

Etsy laid off about 220 people, or 12% of its workforce, as it attempts to simplify its organizational structure. The cuts primarily affected the product and engineering teams, and Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said that the layoffs were necessary to build "the organization we believe Etsy needs for the future." An Etsy spokesperson told CNBC that the cuts were not driven by artificial intelligence adoption.

Microsoft has begun another round of layoffs that affects 4,800 jobs , or around 2.1% of its workforce. The Xbox division is getting hit the hardest, with 3,200 roles getting cut through fiscal year 2027, Xbox chief Asha Sharma said in a post on X — 1,600 people were let go on July 6. Shortly after those layoffs were revealed, it was announced that Sharma was appointed to a U.S. Federal Reserve task force to help advise it on "productivity and jobs." Other appointees include Marc Andreessen of Andreessen Horowitz and Charles I. Jones, professor of economics at Stanford University.

Intel is reportedly downsizing its data center group, despite strong performance. The company hasn't disclosed how many roles would be affected.

Visa will be cutting about 2,600 jobs, which amounts to about 7% of its workforce. The layoffs will primarily affect the technology and product teams, and the impetus in part is to make the company more efficient. "To capture the opportunities ahead and best position Visa to lead this transformation, we must continue evolving how we work," Chief Executive Officer Ryan McInerney wrote in a memo. "AI is also helping to accelerate this evolution and shape the way work gets done at Visa." But according to Bloomberg's report, AI was not the only factor to influence Visa's decision to do these layoffs. The company reportedly intends to reinvest in things like consumer payments and value-added services like stablecoin.

Software company Monday.com will be laying off 20% of its workforce, which comes out to about 630 people. This comes as the company makes a pivot to AI and is attempting to make its AI platform a core offering of its business. Earlier this year, it designed its main product around the idea that business customers increasingly want its employees to work with AI agents.

Patreon laid off 20% of its workforce, or 93 people, as a result of the company "changing our organizational structure and how we work." But Patreon was explicit in its email to creators and staff that "we are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans." However, the email also said "AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, though, including how we work."

Uber has reportedly laid off 10% of its customer service division, according to a Bloomberg report, as it looks to "embrace artificial intelligence" and simplify its ranks. The company also stated in May that it would slow hiring as it makes use of AI more internally.

Samsung is eliminating 179 jobs as it moves its New Jersey headquarters to Texas later this year. The move is expected to impact around 1,000 workers. We're now getting a fuller picture of what that looks like: according to Reuters , 739 roles at Samsung's New Jersey location have been affected in some way. Some have been offered relocation packages as the company shifts its headquarters to Texas, while others have been let go. In addition, it's reported that 100 roles in its Texas location, primarily in the mobile division, have also been let go.

Amazon will lay off some people in its artificial general intelligence group, although the company has not disclosed how many roles will be affected. "This is a fast-moving space, and we're sharpening our focus on the initiatives that matter most for customers, so we can move faster on what counts," an Amazon spokesperson told CNBC.

Sony Interactive Entertainment released a statement that it's cutting "a significant number of employees" from its Bungie workforce. That includes most of the Destiny team and some Marathon team members, as well as SIE teams that support Bungie's operations. The email didn't say how many employees were affected.

Electric vehicle maker Lucid announced it's cutting around 18% of its workforce, and also noted COO Marc Winterhoff's leaving the company, Reuters reported . The layoffs are in an effort to "​boost profitability amid growing competition." The cuts affect full-time employees, contractors and hourly manufacturing workers.

Cloud computing services company Rackspace laid off 750 workers , or around 15% of its workforce. The cuts are driven by a shift in focus toward AI.

EV company Rivian let go of hundreds of employees , which amounts to around 2% of the company's workforce, the Wall Street Journal reported . Those affected were part of Rivian's service and customer organization, which handled marketing and sales.

Trading platform company Robinhood is planning to lay off 10% of its staff to restructure, the Robinhood Comms account shared on X today — that's around 290 jobs. It's unclear if the layoffs are AI-related, but CEO Vlad Tenev noted the company will be "utilizing frontier technologies to push our execution even further."

Salesforce laid off at least 86 employees in California, though Business Insider sources say job cuts also occurred in Washington and outside the U.S. as well. The cuts reportedly affect employees involved with Salesforce's Agentforce AI product, Mulesoft IT integration tool and its Marketing Cloud software.

Groupon is planning to lay off roughly 25% of its workforce , which will result in 400 job cuts. Those positions are expected to be eliminated by the end of the third quarter. This is in an effort to restructure the company and rebuild it as an AI-native company.

In another set of AI-related layoffs, website builder Wix said it was cutting around 20% of staff. Wix cofounder and CEO Avishai Abrahami announced the cuts on X , pointing to the changes AI is bringing to the industry and stating "we need to become a faster, leaner, and flatter organization." He also put part of the blame on the Israeli Shekel to U.S. Dollar exchange rates, which impact the company because it's based in Israel. The cuts are expected to impact around 1,000 roles, based on Wix's headcount.

Webflow, a website builder and hosting company, conducted a round of layoffs that an employee called "a bloodbath" in a statement to the San Francisco Chronicle . It's unclear how many employees were impacted, but one anonymous developer from the company told the Chronicle they believe it was larger than Webflow's last major round of layoffs, which affected 8% of its workforce in 2024. As with other recent layoffs, it looks like a shift to AI is to blame here. "AI is rewriting the rules for how marketing teams create, test, and optimize digital experiences," CEO Linda Tong said in a statement . "And the companies that move decisively through moments like this are the ones that come out ahead."

ClickUp CEO Zeb Evans announced that the company cut 22% of its workforce as it turns toward AI to improve productivity. He claimed it "wasn't about cutting costs," but about funneling savings from the cuts "directly back into the people who stay." The company has introduced million-dollar salary bands reserved for employees who "create outsized impact using AI."

Intuit is planning to lay off 3,000 employees, or about 17% of its workforce, Reuters reports . CEO Sasan Goodarzi sent a memo to employees noting the layoffs would help the company's efforts of focusing on infusing AI across its services.

Meta has officially begun cutting 10% of its workforce , totaling around 8,000 employees. In addition, it plans to close 6,000 open roles. The reason is to allow more room for AI spending.

Like Microsoft, NPR is offering voluntary buyouts to 300 employees in the newsroom, but only 30 will be accepted. However, if the news organization doesn't receive its target number, it will result in targeted layoffs. The reason is due to the loss of federal funding.

The online retail giant cut more jobs this month, this time from the Selling Partner Services organization. These new layoffs come after Amazon cut roughly 30,000 jobs in rounds across October and January. A spokesperson told Business Insider that the most recent layoffs have affected a "small number" of employees. The Selling Partner Services team works with third-party merchants on Amazon, providing onboarding, logistics and account management support.

Cisco is cutting just under 4,000 jobs in Q4, CEO Chuck Robbins said in a blog post . Impacted employees will receive pro-rated payment of 2026 bonuses and will also receive "support in finding new opportunities" via Cisco's placement services. In June, it was confirmed that the layoffs include 471 workers in the Bay Area .

"While we are reducing roles in some areas, we are making clear, strategic investments — particularly in silicon, optics, security, and in our employees' use of AI across the company," Robbins said.

LinkedIn is planning to lay off 5% of its staff, which is around 875 employees, Reuters reports . An anonymous person told Reuters the reason is to reorganize teams and focus employees on areas ⁠where its business is growing. However, one of the sources said the reason was "not for artificial intelligence to replace jobs at LinkedIn."

GM is letting go of around 500 to 600 employees in the Information Technology sector, Bloomberg reports . The reason is to "trim costs and clear the way to bring in staff with skills in other technology areas."

Due to restructuring driven by AI, Cloudflare is cutting more than 1,100 employees . "Today's actions are not a cost-cutting exercise or an assessment of individuals' performance; They are about Cloudflare defining how a world-class, high-growth company operates and creates value in the agentic AI era," Prince and President Michelle Zatlyn said in an email to employees .

PayPal is planning to cut around 20% of its staff — nearly 4,800 employees — over the next few years, according to the Wall Street Journal . "First, we will remove duplication and layers from our organizational structure. Second, we will accelerate our AI adoption and automation across our operations," CEO Enrique Lores said to investors.

Cryptocurrency platform Coinbase is laying off 700 employees , which amounts to around 14% of its staff. CEO Brian Armstrong cites the current market and AI changing the way they work as reasons for the layoffs.

Microsoft is offering a first-ever buyout to up to 7% of its employees, CNBC reports . It's a one-time retirement program that's available for workers at the senior director level and below whose years of employment and age are 70 or higher.

Nike announced it's laying off 1,400 people this week. "Collectively, these changes will result in a reduction of approximately 1,400 roles in global operations, with the majority in technology," COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy said. "These reductions are very hard for the teammates directly affected and for the teams around them, too."

Amazon is planning to temporarily close a warehouse in Homestead, Florida, which will eliminate more than 600 jobs, Newsweek reports . The job cuts will start in July and continue through September but the giant company is giving employees the option to relocate to other facilities. The warehouse has only been open for just under two years but Amazon is already looking to update the site.

Battery recycling company Redwood Materials laid off 10% of its employees, totaling 135 people, TechCrunch reports . Those who were let go received an email from the chief HR officer telling them the layoffs were made "to sharpen our focus, our work and the size of our teams to support the direction Redwood is going in the future."

Snap is laying off 1,000 workers , which is 16% of its staff, Variety reports . The Snapchat parent company made the announcement just weeks after Irenic Capital Management asked the company to make changes to improve performance and revenue.

Snap is using AI to streamline operations and assist the now smaller workforce. "We have already witnessed small squads leveraging AI tools to drive meaningful progress across several important initiatives," Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said.

Just two months after taking over as CEO of Disney, Josh D'Amaro announced the company is laying off 1,000 of its employees, AP News reports . In addition, Marvel let 8% of its staff go after the call was made.

"Over the past several months, we have looked at ways in which we can streamline our operations in various parts of the company to ensure we deliver the world-class creativity and innovation our fans value and expect from Disney," D'Amaro said in a memo to employees. "Given the fast-moving pace of our industries, this requires us to constantly assess how to foster a more agile and technologically-enabled workforce to meet tomorrow's needs."

The wearable camera maker this year will eliminate 145 employees due to a restructuring plan to cut costs, the Wall Street Journal reported . The cuts are expected to last until the end of the year.

Vimeo is going through its third round of layoffs since it was acquired by Bending Spoons. This time, the company let go of more than 120 people, which is about 25% of its city staff .

It's been reported that 200 Meta employees in the Bay Area will lose their jobs at the end of May. That includes 124 employees in Burlingame and 74 in Sunnyvale. The company last laid off workers just a few weeks ago.

Oracle has begun implementing a big cull of its employee base . On the final day of March, more than a dozen Oracle employees announced on LinkedIn they had been let go from their jobs, Business Insider reports . It's unclear at this time how many workers were affected, but it was projected to be thousands at the start of this month.

Those laid off received the same email : "After careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change."

The job cuts are reportedly to help Oracle stem a cash drain related its expenditures on AI infrastructure. In June, Oracle revealed that it had laid off 21,000 people as part of the cuts.

Deux Ex studio Eidos-Montréal announced on March 30 that it's laying off 124 people . In response, the studio head David Anfossi has decided to leave the company.

The cuts are a result of "changing project needs and impacts across production and support teams," the gaming company said in a LinkedIn post . It also noted that the decision to lay off these employees is not related to their talent or performance.

After already having layoffs in January , T-Mobile has cut even more of its workers, GeekWire reports . It's unclear how many people were laid off at this time, but it could be in the hundreds.

"To move even faster in a dynamic market while continuing to deliver best-in-class digital experiences for our customers, we're further aligning our IT organization to support future growth and innovation… This includes the difficult decision of eliminating some roles while continuing to invest and hire in areas," T-Mobile told GeekWire in a statement.

Meta began laying off hundreds of employees on March 25, totaling around 700 people, per The New York Times . Those impacted were part of the Reality Labs team, as well as social media and recruiting teams. Though still significant, this is a much smaller number compared to a Reuters report that suggested 20% off staff would be affected by layoffs due to the increased spending on AI.

This change comes as the company is shifting away from its metaverse creation, which includes Horizon Worlds for its Quest VR headset that's operated by the Reality Labs team.

The gaming giant on March 24 announced it was laying off more than 1,000 workers in an effort to right-size the staff of its popular free-to-play online shooter, Fortnite. CEO Tim Sweeney sent a note to his staff, citing the reason for the layoffs is due to the "downturn in Fortnite engagement," which means "we're spending significantly more than we're making, and we have to make major cuts to keep the company funded." He made it a point to note the layoffs are not related to AI.

105 employees from the Red Storm Entertainment team were laid off by Ubisoft in an effort to cut costs, IGN reports . Game development has ended at the studio, so the downsizing will remain permanent. The company employed 180 people in 2022 but has seen multiple layoffs over the years.

Roughly 1,600 employees were laid off at Atlassian on March 16, which is around 10% of total workers. Ahead of the layoffs, Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes shared a message with the entire team, letting them know the reason is to "self-fund further investment in AI and enterprise sales, while strengthening our financial profile. We're also changing the way we work and reorganising around our System of Work to move faster." Impacted employees received an email shortly after this message went out.

articles.title: Chinese Coast Guard rams Philippine boat in South China Sea, sparking diplomatic clash
articles.summary: A Chinese Coast Guard vessel collided with a Philippine government ship in the South China Sea Friday, sparking a diplomatic dispute between Beijing, Manila and the U.S.
articles.body: Tensions in the South China Sea escalated again Friday after a Chinese Coast Guard vessel collided with a Philippine government ship, an encounter captured on video that prompted competing accounts from Manila and Beijing. The Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat was distributing fuel to Filipino fishermen when the collision occurred at 11:13 a.m., roughly 54 nautical miles off the coast of Palawan province — an area Manila says is well within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone. Footage released by the Philippine Coast Guard showed crew members shouting, "Brace for impact!" moments before the collision. Photographs taken afterward showed bent and detached railings, damaged metal supports and debris scattered across the Philippine ship's deck. No injuries were reported. SEE IT: CHINESE NATIONALS INTERCEPTED IN ‘EXTREMELY DANGEROUS’ INFILTRATION ATTEMPT NEAR FLORIDA COAST Philippine officials accused Beijing of deliberately ramming a civilian government vessel on what they described as a humanitarian and livelihood mission. Jay Tarriela, the Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for West Philippine Sea concerns, said the Chinese vessel first cut across the Philippine ship's stern at a distance of about 33 feet before repeating the maneuver minutes later and colliding with it. Beijing disputed Manila's account. Chinese Coast Guard spokesperson Jiang Lue said the Philippine vessel "intentionally adjusted its course and suddenly accelerated to cut across the bow" of the Chinese ship after disregarding repeated warnings. China said its vessel had been conducting lawful operations near Sabina Shoal and blamed the Philippine side for the collision. The incident also drew Washington into the dispute. U.S. Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said the United States "strongly condemn[s] the China Coast Guard's deliberate ramming." The Chinese Embassy in Manila responded by accusing the United States of backing Philippine "infringement and provocations" in the disputed waters. In July, Manila accused Chinese forces of firing water cannons at government vessels near Scarborough Shoal and striking a Philippine Navy staff member in the head with a wooden baton during an encounter at Second Thomas Shoal.

articles.title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
articles.summary: The coordinated bombings in April 2019 were carried out at three tourist hotels and three churches, killing 279 people.
articles.body:
Sri Lanka’s High Court has convicted 15 of the 24 men accused of being involved in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed 279 people, including 45 foreigners, and injured more than 500.

After a five-year trial, the three-judge bench on Tuesday found that 14 of the accused were guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit “terrorism” and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.

A 15th defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, while nine others were acquitted.

All of the accused are from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community. Twenty-five men were originally charged, but one defendant died in custody.

Among those convicted on all charges was Mohamed Naufar, whom prosecutors identified as the ringleader who provided support to the eight-member squad that carried out the bombings.

The presiding judge told a packed courtroom that sentencing would take place later on Tuesday. Dozens of police commandos provided security outside as the verdicts were read.

Sri Lanka’s Roman Catholic Church welcomed the convictions. “Finally, we have justice,” Catholic priest Jude Fernando told the AFP news agency. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.”

Teresa Fernando, a survivor who suffered head injuries, said no one should have to endure what she had gone through. “We came here today as victims of this attack to receive justice,” she said. “Whatever the court says… we will bow our heads and accept it.”

The coordinated bombings in April 2019 were carried out at three luxury hotels and three churches – two of them Catholic and one Protestant.

A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks.

Two Sri Lanka-based armed groups were accused of carrying out the bombings.

Sri Lanka’s Catholic Church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks.

In July, a former police chief and a former senior Defence Ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror's lawyer torches 'Looney Tunes motion' to investigate him
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's defense seeks an investigation into the holdout juror, while his attorney fires back calling the motion an attack on the Constitution.
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy's defense team is calling for an investigation into the holdout juror who sought to find her guilty of murder in the strangling of her children and using his refusal to bow to peer pressure to ask a judge to dismiss her charges — prompting a blistering response from his lawyer. "The 'Looney Tunes' motion filed yesterday by Kevin 'Shooter McGavin' Reddington to investigate Michael is not just an attack on Michael for being the courageous lone holdout juror," attorney Edward Paltzik wrote on X Tuesday morning, referring to the holdout, Michael Desronvil. "Reddington's motion is actually a full-frontal attack on the U.S. Constitution," Paltzik warned. "Because if the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye." LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN He warned that if the judge grants defense demands for an investigation into his client it would undermine the American criminal justice system in the long run. "If we follow his destructive proposal to its logical conclusion, we're going to have an endless cycle of prosecutors investigating holdouts who oppose 'guilty' and defense attorneys investigating holdouts who oppose 'not guilty,'" he wrote. "Pretty soon we'll end up with... a retrograde justice system that will look a lot like the Hatfield-McCoy Feud: a cycle of carnage so malignant that its origins will fade in importance, replaced by the hopeless death spiral of the cycle itself." Reddington, in a motion filed Friday, called for a "limited inquiry" into the holdout, for information about his background and potential criminal history, phone records, courthouse surveillance video and more. Neither Paltzik nor Reddington immediately responded to requests for comment from Fox News Digital Tuesday morning. LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL In a separate filing, another attorney for Clancy, Martin Weinberg, argued that Judge William Sullivan's decision to overrule a defense objection at trial should be grounds for dismissing the charges against the 36-year-old defendant on double jeopardy grounds. That motion also centered on the holdout juror and allegations that he ignored the judge's instructions and the law. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "The jury twice informed the Court that one of its members was refusing to apply the Court's instructions regarding the fundamental concept of reasonable doubt," Weinberg wrote. "After the first such report, the Court asked each juror individually whether he or she was able to apply the law. Upon receiving the second report, the Court tempered its response even further, simply reminding all jurors as a group of their obligation to follow its instructions generally. The Court denied Ms. Clancy's explicit requests to go further." LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR MAKES NEW PROMISE AS LAWYER WARNS OF PUBLIC ATTACKS SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Weinberg's motion argued that Sullivan's decision to declare a mistrial before investigating the holdout is improper, alleging that the jury foreperson accused the holdout of making "statements acknowledging doubt but refus[ing] to apply it to the verdict as the law states." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE Paltzik has said he began representing Desronvil last week as the holdout faced mounting public pressure from his fellow jurors, Clancy's defense and her supporters among the public. JUROR ON LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL SAYS 'WE LET DOWN LINDSAY' FOLLOWING MISTRIAL Several other jurors have spoken publicly following Clancy's mistrial, which was declared on Sept. 4. Some, including the jury foreperson, have accused Desronvil of ignoring his own reasonable doubts about the prosecution's case, a claim he denied in his only public remarks. GOT A TIP? "I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement last week, first made to NewsNation. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present." LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST He said that based on the physical evidence, witness testimony and the prosecution's presentations, he "thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned." GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, admitted killing her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — but argued she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Prosecutors argued she planned the murders and understood that what she was doing was wrong. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29.

articles.title: Romania is exploring whether European mink could return to the Carpathians, where the species has disappeared from much of its former range
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Conservation organisations in Romania and across Europe are assessing whether the critically endangered European mink could eventually be returned to .
articles.body: Conservation organisations in Romania and across Europe are assessing whether the critically endangered European mink could eventually be returned to parts of the southern Carpathian Mountains, where the species has disappeared from much of its former range. The work is currently at the feasibility and planning stage, with researchers assessing habitat suitability, landscape connectivity, potential threats and the condition of Romania's remaining European mink population in the Danube Delta. The Vincent Wildlife Trust is working with the Romanian Wilderness Society, Fauna & Flora, and the Danube Delta National Institute for Research and Development to determine whether conservation translocations could be a viable means of restoring European mink populations in the Carpathians. No mink have been released as part of this project. Instead, researchers are gathering the information needed to establish whether a future translocation could be carried out without putting the Danube Delta population at risk. The initiative forms part of wider efforts to conserve the species and the freshwater habitats on which it depends.The European mink has disappeared from most of its former rangeThe European mink (Mustela lutreola) is one of Europe's most threatened mammals. Its distribution has contracted dramatically since the 19th century, and the species now occupies less than 20% of its former range, according to the Vincent Wildlife Trust. European mink survive in a small number of isolated areas, including parts of France and Spain and the Danube Delta region of Romania and Ukraine. Conservation programmes have also established or supported populations in some areas where the species had disappeared.The decline has been linked to several factors, including historical hunting for fur, the loss and degradation of wetlands and river habitats, pollution and the spread of the American mink (Neogale vison). The American mink can compete with European mink for food and habitat and is considered an important threat to the species. In Romania, the only confirmed remaining population is in the Danube Delta in southeastern Romania. It is considered an important stronghold for European mink in Europe, but researchers are also working to establish how large and secure the population actually is.Researchers are mapping potential routes through the southern CarpathiansThe Romanian project is not yet a reintroduction programme in the sense of animals being released into the wild. Its first stage is to determine whether the southern Carpathians contain suitable connected habitat for a future conservation translocation. Researchers have used remotely sensed data and ecological information to model functional connectivity across 3 areas of the southern Carpathians being considered for potential reintroduction. The modelling is designed to show where European mink could potentially move through the landscape and identify barriers, including roads and other infrastructure.Field surveys are being used to ground-truth and refine the modelling results. They also provide an opportunity to investigate whether American mink are present in areas being assessed for European mink conservation. The work was presented at the 35th European Mustelid Colloquium, held in Cluj-Napoca in September 2024. Patrick Wright presented “A journey towards restoring the European mink to the Romanian Carpathians” during the conference's lightning-talk programme, providing an overview of the restoration work.The Danube Delta population must be assessed before any animals are movedA future translocation would also depend on the condition of Romania's remaining European mink population in the Danube Delta. Researchers are combining existing information with targeted field surveys to assess the population's distribution and abundance. This is important because animals for a conservation translocation would need to come from a suitable source population. The feasibility work therefore considers whether the Danube Delta population is sufficiently large and robust to support the removal of animals without compromising its own long-term survival.The project's feasibility assessment is also examining potential conservation approaches rather than committing to a single release strategy. Any future decision would have to take into account the condition of the source population, the availability of suitable habitat and the threats facing European mink at potential release sites. The Danube Delta assessment is particularly important because the precise conservation status of the European mink population there remains an area of investigation. Establishing its distribution and abundance will help determine whether conservation translocation is appropriate.A future reintroduction would depend on the feasibility findingsFor European mink to return to the southern Carpathians, several conditions would need to be met. Researchers would need evidence of suitable habitat, sufficient landscape connectivity and manageable threats at potential release sites. The availability and long-term security of animals from an appropriate source population would also have to be established. The project is therefore focused on building the evidence needed for a future decision rather than announcing a confirmed reintroduction. If the feasibility work supports translocation, further planning would still be required before animals could be moved.The project also contributes to broader conservation planning for European mink in Romania, with the Danube Delta National Institute for Research and Development involved in work on the species and its conservation. For now, the proposed return of European mink to the Carpathians remains a conservation possibility under investigation. The current work is focused on determining whether the landscape, the remaining Romanian population and the conditions at potential release sites could support a viable future restoration effort.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Venezuelan man shot by ICE officer was taken to detention with ‘bullet lodged near his spine’, lawyer claims
articles.summary: US News: A Venezuelan man shot by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Texas was taken to an immigration detention facility with a bullet .
articles.body: A Venezuelan man shot by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Texas was taken to an immigration detention facility with a bullet still lodged in his back near his spine, his lawyer said, as new details emerged about his condition.His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was later taken back to a hospital and has lost movement on the left side of his body.According to CNN, Lincoln-Goldfinch said Perez was transported to an ICE facility about 100 miles away after being shot, despite the bullet remaining lodged in his back.She said her client had not received adequate medical treatment while in detention and was in significant pain.Perez was shot on Sunday while making a DoorDash delivery in Austin, Texas. His lawyer said ICE agents sideswiped his vehicle before an agent opened fire. Perez was initially taken to a hospital before being released into ICE custody, according to The Hill.Lawyer disputes ICE accountLincoln-Goldfinch said Perez did not try to evade the officers and was attempting to find a place to pull over. She alleged that agents did not initially use lights or sirens and that the shooting happened after the vehicles collided.Perez, speaking by phone from the Pearsall Detention Facility during a news conference, said he was in severe pain and that doctors had not removed the bullet because it was too close to his spine.The lawyer said Perez was later hospitalized again on Monday night. She has also sought his release from detention so he can receive medical treatment while recovering from the gunshot wound.Investigation underwayThe Department of Homeland Security is leading the investigation into the shooting. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the department would allow evidence, rather than speculation or incomplete information, to guide the investigation.US Rep Greg Casar, who represents the Austin area where the shooting occurred, has called for the release of body-camera footage and a full investigation. Dozens of protesters also gathered near the scene, with some carrying Mexican and Guatemalan flags and signs calling for ICE to leave Austin.The shooting comes amid increased scrutiny of ICE operations in the US following several incidents involving federal immigration agents. DHS has said Perez is in federal custody pending removal from the country, while his lawyer and Casar have disputed parts of the government's account of his immigration status.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Mahindra Thar OG launched: Prices, variants, features and more
articles.summary: Cars News: Mahindra has launched the new Thar OG, bringing a substantial update to its three-door lifestyle SUV. Prices start at Rs 10.32 lakh, ex-showroom, whil.
articles.body: Mahindra has launched the new Thar OG, bringing a substantial update to its three-door lifestyle SUV. Prices start at Rs 10.32 lakh, ex-showroom, while deliveries are scheduled to begin from October 11, 2026. The new model gets a new platform, revised suspension, more powerful engine options, additional safety features and styling changes.The Thar OG is based on Mahindra’s M_Glyde 4G platform, which is claimed to offer higher stiffness for improved on-road and off-road driving characteristics. The SUV also gets DAVINCI Damping technology with Frequency Dependent Damping (FDD) and a rear PENTALINK suspension with Watts Link.The SUV now comes with Electric Power Steering, which is aimed at making manoeuvring easier, particularly at lower speeds. Mahindra has also worked on NVH levels, with the company claiming improved refinement inside the cabin.Mahindra Thar OG: Engine optionsThe Thar OG gets three engine options. The 2.0-litre G20 TGDi mStallion petrol engine produces 119 kW and 330 Nm, while the 2.2-litre D22 mHawk diesel develops 111.9 kW and 330 Nm. The D117 CRDe diesel continues to produce 87.2 kW and 300 Nm.Depending on the variant and powertrain, the Thar OG is available with rear-wheel drive and four-wheel drive. The 4WD versions get an Electronic Locking Differential and dedicated Mud, Sand and Snow Terrain Modes. RWD versions with the 2.2-litre mHawk and 2.0-litre mStallion engines also get Terrain Assist.Thar OG gets styling and cabin updatesThe overall boxy silhouette of the Thar has been retained, but Mahindra has made several design changes. The SUV gets a new grille, LED headlamps with signature C-shaped DRLs, LED fog lamps with cornering function and new LED tail lamps. It also gets revised front and rear bumpers and new R19 alloy wheels on higher variants.The Thar OG is offered in two new exterior colours, Artemis Silver and Jeans Blue, along with six existing colour options. Inside, the SUV gets Truffle Brown leatherette upholstery and a soft second-row armrest with integrated cupholders.Other features include a 26.03 cm HD touchscreen infotainment system, colour MID, cruise control, rear AC vents, rear wiper and washer, wireless charging and Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The SUV also gets washable flooring with drain plugs on 4WD variants.Six airbags now standardSafety is another area where the Thar OG gets a major update. Six airbags and all-four disc brakes are now offered, with the airbag package including four Head Pelvis Thorax Shoulder (HPTS) airbags for front and rear occupantsThe SUV also gets an ESP 9.3 suite, including rollover mitigation, traction control, hill-hold control and vehicle dynamics control. Higher variants get front parking sensors and a rear-view camera, while a tyre pressure monitoring system is also available.Mahindra Thar OG price and variantsThe Thar OG is available in AXT, LXT and ZXT variants. The entry-level AXT is priced at Rs 10.32 lakh and is available with the D117 CRDe diesel engine, RWD and a manual gearbox.The LXT variant starts at Rs 12.99 lakh for the D117 CRDe diesel RWD manual and goes up to Rs 18.00 lakh, depending on the powertrain and configuration. The ZXT range starts at Rs 13.99 lakh and goes up to Rs 18.99 lakh.These are introductory prices and are valid for deliveries made until November 30, 2026.

articles.title: ‘American Idol’ contestant’s murder case sent cops underground with high-powered magnet to find gun
articles.summary: Caleb Flynn's murder trial revealed how Ohio investigators searched storm drains, attics and vehicles for the gun allegedly used to kill Ashley Flynn.
articles.body: Former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn's missing handgun sent investigators into storm drains with a high-powered magnet, underneath vehicles and through attic insulation as they searched for the weapon prosecutors allege he used to kill his wife. Despite the extensive search, investigators never found the gun, a Tipp City detective testified Monday during Flynn's murder trial in Ohio. Flynn is accused of fatally shooting his wife, Ashley Flynn, inside the couple's home on Feb. 16 before staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY The trial turned deeply personal Tuesday as Ashley's mother and sister took the stand, describing the family's frantic first hours after her death and the stunning revelation that Flynn had allegedly been having an affair with a woman they knew from church. Ashley's mother, Jill Smith, testified that her phone rang around 3 a.m. the morning her daughter was killed. She initially thought it was her husband, who was traveling, but saw Flynn's name on the screen instead. "She's gone," Smith recalled Flynn telling her. When Smith asked who he meant, Flynn responded, "Ashley, she's gone," before telling her, "Someone broke in and shot her," she testified. Smith said she told Flynn she was coming to the house, but he told her police were there and she could not come. She hung up, became dizzy and lay down on the bathroom floor. "It seemed like forever," Smith testified, saying she remained there for about five minutes before getting up and calling her husband to tell him Ashley had been killed. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY Smith drove to the home anyway and said seeing the flashing police lights made the reality of what had happened sink in. "And then I knew it was true," she testified. Flynn later came outside shaking, Smith said. The two hugged before sitting on the front porch, where she became concerned enough about him that she asked for a blanket and suggested someone call an EMT because she feared he was going into shock. Ashley's sister, Kayla Keyt, testified that she initially believed so strongly in Flynn's innocence that she told investigators "100%" they had arrested the wrong man. "I trusted Caleb with everything I had in me," Keyt testified. Keyt said she became angry when she initially heard rumors that Flynn had been having an affair because she believed they were unfairly damaging his reputation. "I was so mad because it was tarnishing his reputation," Keyt said. "I just knew in my heart that he was completely innocent. I really believed that with all of my heart." Keyt testified that changed when investigators told her Flynn had been having an affair with Alleigha, a woman the family knew from Christian Life Center. Alleigha was the church's main worship leader and performed alongside Flynn, who sang with the worship team during rehearsals and weekend services, Keyt testified. She said she personally knew Alleigha casually from seeing her at church. "I don't think I've been more shocked in my life," Keyt said. Keyt recalled asking investigators, "Are you 100% sure?" and said she had them repeat it two or three times because she "could not even fathom" Flynn having an affair. She testified that she first learned about it during an FBI interview the morning after Flynn's arrest. Keyt, who testified that Ashley's two daughters now live with her family, said the girls have since learned about the alleged affair and personally knew Alleigha. "They were mostly brokenhearted for mommy," Keyt testified. Keyt said the girls were shocked and questioned why their father did not love their mother as much as Ashley loved him. But when the girls were told who Flynn had allegedly been involved with, Keyt recalled the older daughter's response: "I'm not surprised." The emotional testimony Tuesday followed a day of forensic evidence and testimony about investigators' exhaustive search for the missing gun. Detective Adam Bernard walked jurors through the lengths investigators went to as they searched for the missing firearm in the days after Ashley's death. Police searched the backyard and nearby wooded areas before turning their attention underground, where investigators used a high-powered magnet to search storm drains along several streets. Bernard testified that investigators removed the drain covers, lowered the magnet inside and swept connecting pipes before he physically climbed into accessible culverts with a flashlight to search areas the magnet may have missed. They found nothing. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY Investigators later had both vehicles from the Flynn home placed on lifts so they could search underneath them and other areas where something could have been hidden, Bernard testified. That search also came up empty. Police even rented equipment to remove insulation from the attic as they continued looking for the gun. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY Bernard testified that investigators also tried to trace Flynn's firearm purchase history after Flynn previously said he bought a gun in South Carolina, where he obtained his concealed-carry permit. The detective said he called nearly two dozen gun stores in the state looking for records that could identify the make, model and serial number of a firearm purchased by Flynn. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY That effort did not identify a gun tied to Flynn or Ashley. The testimony came after a forensic pathologist walked jurors through Ashley's autopsy and described two gunshot wounds to the back of her head. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY Dr. Bryan Casto testified that the entrance wounds overlapped, and the bullets traveled through Ashley's head on nearly parallel paths. One of the bullets exited her head before reentering her left arm near the elbow, where it was recovered during the autopsy. Casto said the wounds and the paths of the bullets suggested Ashley was shot at close range, but he could not say exactly how far away the gun was when it was fired. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY The pathologist determined Ashley died from multiple gunshot wounds to the head. Earlier Monday, Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation (BCI) crime scene investigators walked jurors through evidence collected throughout the Flynn home as prosecutors sought to show the alleged break-in had been staged. ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY A BCI crime scene technician who had examined between 20 and 30 forced-entry doors testified that the damage to a side garage door did not look like the forced entries she had previously investigated. She said the damage was on the inside of the door rather than areas she would typically expect to be damaged if someone had kicked or pried their way inside. articles.title: In 1995, former NYSE CEO John Thain bought a Westchester estate for $3.7 million; the roughly 10-acre property carries five addresses and stretches across three New York municipalities
articles.summary: US News: A 10-acre estate in Westchester County, New York, owned by former New York Stock Exchange boss John Thain, is so large it stretches across three diffe.
articles.body: A 10-acre estate in Westchester County, New York, owned by former New York Stock Exchange boss John Thain, is so large it stretches across three different towns and has five separate street addresses. The property at 350 Purchase St. sits across the borders of the City of Rye, the Village of Rye Brook, and the Town of Harrison. Public records show the main house is 13,172 square feet, sitting on a lot of about 438,000 square feet. Built in 1910, it's one of the few private homes in the area split across three separate local governments, according to local news outlet Rye-Harrison News. Thain and his wife, Carmen, bought the estate in 1995 for $3.7 million. A November 2007 report by the New York Post described the full scale of the 14-bedroom mansion. At that time, the property had two swimming pools, a clay tennis court, several beehives, and a private stream running through the backyard that fed into a lake stocked with fish. Property records show Thain has been listed at the address since at least 2006, and federal election filings have regularly listed a Rye address for him.Local impact and taxesOwning a property that crosses town lines creates some unusual paperwork. By 2007, tax records cited by the New York Post showed Thain was paying more than $150,000 a year combined to the Town of Harrison and the City of Rye. More recent tax figures for the property were not publicly available. The sheer size of the estate has drawn comments from neighbors over the years. In a 2007 interview with the New York Post, one neighbor described just how big the grounds are. "The place is huge. I have seen him riding around the perimeter... it probably takes him 20 minutes to get from the front gate to the back," the neighbor told the outlet. The property came back into local attention on Sept. 19, when community website MyRye.com featured Thain in a profile series about notable local residents.Career on Wall StreetBefore buying the Westchester estate, Thain built a long career at the top levels of American finance. He spent more than 20 years at Goldman Sachs, eventually becoming president and co-chief operating officer. In 2004, he became CEO of the New York Stock Exchange, leading the organization until 2007. He then became chairman and CEO of Merrill Lynch just as the 2008 financial crisis began. While there, he negotiated the firm's $50 billion sale to Bank of America, a deal announced on Sept. 15, 2008, during the height of the banking crisis. His time at Merrill Lynch ended suddenly in early 2009 after public backlash over bonus payments made to executives right before the merger was finalized. After leaving Wall Street, commercial lender CIT Group named Thain chairman and CEO in February 2010, according to National Public Radio (NPR). He led the company through its recovery from bankruptcy before retiring from CIT Group in March 2016.Recent board roles and community workBeyond his corporate career, Thain has stayed active in company boards and local conservation work. He joined Uber's board of directors in September 2017, during the company's move toward going public. Thain and his wife also serve on the Board of Managers at the New York Botanical Garden. As major donors, they helped fund the restoration of the garden's 50-acre old-growth forest in the Bronx, which was later named after the family. Despite his business roles in Manhattan and on boards across the country, the Purchase Street estate remains Thain's main home, spread firmly across three different Westchester communities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ex-Rwandan official appears at UK trial over 1994 genocide
articles.summary: Prosecutors allege Vincent Brown incited and directed acts of violence during the early days of the Rwandan genocide.
articles.body:
A former Rwandan official has appeared in a court in the United Kingdom after being charged with ordering six killings during the first week of the Rwandan genocide in 1994.

Vincent Brown, a 65-year-old doctor formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, is the first ⁠person to be charged in Britain over the genocide, in which more than 800,000 people, most from the Tutsi ethnic minority , were killed in over 100 days of nationwide massacres. He denied any wrongdoing.

On Tuesday, Brown spoke in court to confirm his name, date of birth and address. He did not enter a plea.

Brown faces one charge of conduct ancillary to genocide in Rwanda’s capital, Kigali, in April 1994 during the first week of the genocide. The doctor is accused of ordering six killings in four days, including of a young mother and her baby son.

Prosecutor Jane Stansfield said Brown was head of the Department of Family Health within ⁠Rwanda’s National Office of Population when the genocide began.

Originally from Kigali, Brown is believed to have entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998 and lived in London, where he once worked for a charity assisting refugee nurses and midwives seeking work in Britain.

Brown officially changed his last name from Bajinya when granted UK citizenship in 2004 and was first arrested in 2006. His extradition to Rwanda along with four other men was finally refused by a British court in 2017.

The Rwandan government had asked the Metropolitan Police to investigate the men for involvement in killings in the Rugenge district of Kigali that are the focus of Brown’s current trial.

The charges arose after a complex seven-year UK investigation that began in September 2019.

Brown’s lawyer Sam ⁠Blom-Cooper said his client welcomed an opportunity to clear his name. “These are appalling crimes, terrible murders that were committed back in 1994,” he said. “But this, finally, does represent the beginning of the end for Dr Brown.”

Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring granted Brown bail on condition that his family pay 25,000 pounds ($33,000) security. Due to the seriousness of the allegations, he transferred the case to the Central Criminal Court, also known as the Old Bailey, where Brown is due to appear on October 9.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said the trial will set an important precedent against impunity even for decades-old allegations.

“This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes,” she said.
