articles.title: Australia began restoring a damaged swamp forest on former sugarcane land; trees planted less than a year ago grew more than 4 metres
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A former sugarcane property in Far North Queensland is being transformed through an 11-year project to restore endangered lowland rainforest in Babind.
articles.body: A former sugarcane property in Far North Queensland is being transformed through an 11-year project to restore endangered lowland rainforest in Babinda. The Babinda Swamp Forest Restoration project aims to restore wetland vegetation, create habitat for 53 threatened plant and animal species, and improve water quality that flows into the Great Barrier Reef catchment. It is funded through the Queensland Government’s Land Restoration Fund; the $1.5 million project is also intended to generate Australian Carbon Credit Units while supporting local employment and skills. According to a Queensland Government case study on the Babinda Swamp Forest Restoration project, by its second year, 38 hectares of rainforest species had been planted. However, the low-lying site presents challenges for restoration.Babinda project restores lowland rainforest on a sugarcane propertyThe Babinda Swamp Forest Restoration project is re-establishing endangered lowland rainforest in Far North Queensland. The restoration is taking place on sugarcane property through an 11-year, $1.5 million initiative funded by the Queensland Government’s Land Restoration Fund. The project uses reforestation by Environmental or Mallee Plantings. By its second year, 38 hectares of rainforest species had been planted. The project will restore habitat for 53 threatened plant and animal species, improve water quality entering the Great Barrier Reef catchment and strengthen resilience to flooding and a changing climate. The work supports employment and skills development.How rainfall and flooding are affecting Babinda rainforest restorationThe site lies at the base of Queensland’s two tallest mountains, Mount Bartle Frere and Mount Bellenden Kerr, and receives more than four metres of rainfall each year. The planting areas are only two to six metres above sea level, making them prone to flooding and tidal backflow. Conditions during the 2024–25 wet season highlighted the restoration challenge. Around half of the 13 hectares of newly planted area was lost after seedlings were buried under thick layers of plant litter and mud. Rivers stayed above minor flood levels for record lengths of time, while tidal backflow combined with dry-season flooding affected conditions. In some areas, a five-centimetre difference in ground height determined whether seedlings survived there.What changes were made to improve rainforest planting successThe project team revised its restoration approach after the 2024-25 wet season. The team used microtopography mapping, revised species selection and adjusted planting schedules to improve seedling resilience in swamp-like conditions. Project lead Gabrielle Davidson described the changes as continuous adaptive management based on observation and ongoing decision-making. By 2026, the changes, along with a different type of wet season, had produced results in some areas. Trees planted less than a year earlier had already grown more than four metres tall. The project team continues to work in a landscape that is difficult to plan for and maintain. The restoration approach was adjusted to respond to changing wetland conditions.Rainforest restoration brings habitat and employment benefits to BabindaAs the rainforest regenerates, the project will provide habitat for threatened wildlife including estuarine crocodiles, microbats, freshwater fish and frogs, as well as 40 threatened plant species. Planting has improved habitat for the southern cassowary and spectacled flying-fox, along with rare rainforest plants including the erect banana and Russell River Lime, found only in the region.The project is also intended to improve water quality entering the Great Barrier Reef catchment and strengthen resilience to flooding and a changing climate. Twenty-six people have worked on site, including TAFE Conservation and Land Management graduates. Some trainees have progressed into higher-level roles, while local nurseries supply native seedlings and support restoration businesses.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from overdose of fentanyl and other drugs
articles.summary: The death of the child star - who had fentanyl, Xanax, a muscle relaxant and antipsychotic medication in her system -  was ruled an accident.
articles.body:
Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina.

The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death.

Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence.

The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse.

The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions.

Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone.

The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful".

The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death.

Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died.

Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression.

Panettiere has said she was introduced to drugs around the age of 16 during a red carpet appearance for Heroes when a member of her professional team gave her something called a "happy pill" for energy.

"I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction," she told People Magazine. "As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn't live without."

Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition. Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother also struggled with substance abuse and used heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

articles.title: Nolan Wells' friends cleared by grand jury as their lawyers vow to hold online accusers accountable
articles.summary: A Mississippi grand jury found Nolan Wells' death consistent with drowning and no evidence of a crime or racial motive in the Horn Island case.
articles.body: After a Mississippi grand jury found that Nolan Wells' death was "consistent with drowning" and turned up no evidence of a crime or racial motive, an attorney for one of the men wrongly targeted online said his client intends to hold the accusers accountable. Wells, 19, disappeared July 4 after taking a boat trip to Horn Island, a barrier island along Mississippi's Gulf Coast, with a group of friends. Search crews combed the area for two days until a National Park Service ranger discovered his remains at the island's northwestern tip on July 6. Months later, a Jackson County, Mississippi, grand jury returned a "no true bill" in Wells' death investigation, meaning no indictment or charges will be filed. "The Grand Jury finds that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells' remains is consistent with drowning," the grand jury wrote. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Russell Latino, who represents Bart Edmiston and his family, said: "This story involves two tragedies. SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST "The death of Nolan Wells is a tragedy. So too is the way his friends, his community and his state were maligned by unscrupulous charlatans and grifters who spread false and malicious lies," Latino said. "The grand jury, made up of Mississippians of all races and backgrounds, did its solemn duty. But to anyone who knew the actual facts, not reckless garbage spewed on the internet, the result of the process was never in doubt. The Edmiston family looks forward to bringing accountability to those who exploited tragedy to divide and injure. They continue to pray for healing, for the family of Nolan and for their precious community." Edmiston and other friends of Wells' were subjected to months of online rumors and speculation that they were somehow criminally responsible for the then-18-year-old's death. The grand jury and Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath both concluded those allegations were baseless. Edward Andrew Paltzik, who represents three of Wells' friends, had a pointed message for attorney Ben Crump. "@AttorneyCrump NO TRUE BILL. You should apologize immediately to completely innocent young men Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo, and Morgan Seymour. You have some serious explaining to do!" Paltzik said. He said he's also sent several legal notices to social media influencers and media figures on behalf of three men he represents. In a video statement Monday, Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath said there was "absolutely no evidence" that Wells' death was due to his race. Fox News Digital has reached out to Crump for comment. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS "The narrative that three White boys and a Black boy went to an island and only three White friends returned spread like wildfire. This was false," McIlrath said. "There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan's disappearance and death were racially motivated." "Nolan's friends loved Nolan and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that," she said. NOLAN WELLS' HOMETOWN OFFICIALS RALLY BEHIND SHERIFF AFTER 'DERELICT IN THEIR DUTIES' ATTACK READ THE GRAND JURY REPORT: McIlrath also sharply criticized attorney Ben Crump's team, which she said knew early on that the death wasn't racially motivated. "The family, the Crump team, and anyone close to Nolan knew that his disappearance and death were not the result of racial hate or violence," she said. "What I am suggesting is that the Crump team knew better but did not do better." SEND US A TIP According to the district attorney, the family's legal team advised her office in August that it had uncovered no evidence a crime was committed against Wells. "On August 13th, 2026, after the Crump team conducted and released the results of its independent autopsy and after receiving hundreds of tips, they advised my office that they had no evidence of a crime being committed against Nolan Wells," she said. CAJUN NAVY LEADER WARNS NOLAN WELLS' SEARCH AREA HAS DEADLY 'WASHING MACHINE' CURRENTS: 'LOTS OF DROWNINGS' Lawyers representing Wells' family disputed the decision in a statement to Fox News Digital. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump said the state was closing the case before the truth had been established, citing bruising on the back of Wells' head and an independent autopsy that he said documented blunt force injuries to Wells' head and back. Crump said neither the family nor the state has determined how Wells died, and he urged the Justice Department to open an investigation if Mississippi declines to do so. "Today, the State of Mississippi is attempting to close the chapter on Nolan Wells’ death without getting to the truth," Crump said. "We are releasing the final independent autopsy report in its entirety, so everyone can read it for themselves. This grand jury result leaves us with more questions than answers. Nolan’s family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we." LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Both the Mississippi Chief Medical Examiner and the family's pathologist, Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed a second autopsy for the Wells family agreed that while the cause of death is undetermined, "drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion." That means the conclusion was reached by ruling out other causes rather than by direct evidence of drowning. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL The grand jury didn't find any evidence suggesting a crime occurred, or that Wells' death was motivated by race, and also took direct aim at the theories circulating on social media about the people on the boats. GOVERNOR BLAMES ACTIVISTS IN NOLAN WELLS CASE FOR ‘STOKING DIVISION,’ OFFICIAL SAYS FBI PROBING THREATS "The Grand Jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026, on the Triton, the Palm Beach, or the Tideline engaged in any criminal conduct related to the death of Mr. Wells," the grand jury wrote. "The allegations against the occupants of the Triton, the Palm Beach, and the Tideline are not based in truth, and are solely the result of public clamor and private malice." NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS Among the many questions surrounding Wells' death was an apparent injury to the back of his head, where bruising was found. A witness testified that he saw Wells slip off a boat, but the grand jury said it could not confirm the fall caused the bruising. CALIFORNIA MAN ARRESTED FOR ALLEGEDLY SENDING BOMB THREAT TO JUDGE IN NOLAN WELLS' DEATH CASE: DOCS "A witness testified under oath that he saw Mr. Wells slip awkwardly off the side of a boat around the time of 3:30 p.m. on July 4, 2026, but could not say whether Mr. Wells struck his head during the fall. The witness testified that Mr. Wells continued to socialize after the fall and did not appear injured," the grand jury report said. articles.title: 'Looksmaxxing' influencer 'Clavicular' charged with rape in Massachusetts
articles.summary: Authorities allege Braden Peters drugged a woman before assaulting her in May. He denies the charges.
articles.body:
The online influencer "Clavicular", whose real name is Braden Peters, has been charged with rape, providing liquor to a person under the legal US drinking age, and drugging someone for sexual intercourse, court records show.

The alleged offences occurred in May 2025, according to the charges filed in the state of Massachusetts.

A spokesperson for Peters told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the charges are "bogus" and that the influencer has yet to be served with an arrest warrant.

Peters is facing a civil lawsuit filed by a woman earlier this year who alleged that he had served her several rounds of vodka and had nonconsensual sex with her at his parents' home on Cape Cod.

The woman said she was a minor at the time and also accused him of injecting her with a non-FDA approved substance. He denied the allegations.

The criminal charges filed this month do not identify the alleged victim.

Clavicular is known for his role in an online movement called "looksmaxxing", centred on maximising physical attractiveness.

articles.title: Juvenile murder sentence rule doesn't breach human rights, says Supreme Court
articles.summary: The top court rejects an appeal for a minimum term review from a man who was sentenced after turning 18.
articles.body:
Scrapping a law that could have shortened a man's prison sentence because he committed murder as a child was not a breach of human rights, the Supreme Court has ruled.

Jesse Quaye, then 17, and Ayomindy Bile, then 15, murdered Connor Barrett in Hemsby, Norfolk in 2014 - leading to both being jailed for life with a minimum term of 15 years.

But a later change in the law meant Quaye could not ask for a review of that minimum term, because he had turned 18 before he was sentenced.

The Supreme Court's decision to reject his appeal ends the legal battle over juvenile life sentences in the UK courts - but the case could potentially be reopened at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

Connor Barrett, 21, died after he was attacked by Quaye and Ayomindy Bile when they turned up uninvited at a birthday party to assault another attendee.

Their trial heard that the pair had brought knives with them and that their victim died in front of his family, including his younger brother.

After their conviction, Quaye, by then 18, and Bile were jailed at Her Majesty's pleasure - the legal term for a life sentence given to child killers.

Under long-standing legal principles, a juvenile who is sentenced to murder can ask for their minimum term to be reconsidered once they have served half of that time.

That policy and other juvenile sentencing laws take into account evidence that some serious offenders rehabilitate in their 20s as they mature.

However, Parliament voted in 2022 to block juvenile killers from seeking a review if they had been sentenced after they had turned 18.

The new law meant Quaye could no longer ask for a review of his minimum term and the 29-year-old remains in prison, prompting him to mount a legal challenge.

Lawyers for Quaye had argued that his treatment amounted to a breach of the ban on arbitrary detention, retrospective punishment and discrimination based on age in the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).

In 2024, two High Court judges ruled that Quaye's treatment breached those safeguards - but the Court of Appeal later reversed that decision.

In their ruling on Tuesday, the five Supreme Court judges said the law had long differentiated between child and adult killers, and that the trial judge had correctly and fairly decided on a minimum term.

They concluded the ECHR did not compel the UK government to consider reducing Quaye's minimum term.

"The judgement is one of social policy, involving questions of moral and political judgement, which is the province of the legislature [Parliament]," they said.

"Moreover, drawing a bright line distinction based on being 18 at the date of conviction or sentence is a recognised feature of sentencing and the criminal justice system."

Simon Creighton, a leading sentencing law solicitor who represented Quaye, said the case had raised two basic questions of fairness.

"When people receive these particular sentences, they were told that the sentence meant they would have a review," he said.

"To be told a decade later that was no longer the case is one aspect of the unfairness.

"We all know about the lengthy delays in the criminal courts at the moment. And it really is purely arbitrary whether your case is going to come up for trial before you've turned 18 or not.

"To make a decision about what the sentence means, based on something that's so arbitrary and out of people's control, feels like a major injustice."

Creighton said there was a "strong prospect" of asking the European court in Strasbourg to review the outcome.

In general, such cases can take years to be heard and the court only considers appeals when it thinks the courts in the UK have not fully resolved human rights questions.

articles.title: Nigeria prison deaths: Inside the cell where 33 inmates lost their lives
articles.summary: The BBC goes inside the prison where prisoners were trapped in stifling, cramped conditions.
articles.body:
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.

The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.

Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.

The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests , including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.

Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.

"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.

When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.

The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.

"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.

Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.

The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.

Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.

The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.

As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.

He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.

"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."

But no-one came to help, he and others allege.

"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.

"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.

"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."

Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.

The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.

"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.

As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.

A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.

It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.

No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.

As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

articles.title: Philippine forests are being restored without planting every tree; scientists use natural regeneration to bring degraded land back
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Restoring a forest does not always mean planting thousands of seedlings. In the Philippines, researchers are examining assisted natural regeneration (.
articles.body: Restoring a forest does not always mean planting thousands of seedlings. In the Philippines, researchers are examining assisted natural regeneration (ANR), an approach that helps forests recover by protecting and managing trees that return. According to research published in Trees, Forests and People by Science Direct, titled ‘Assisted natural regeneration for tropical forest and landscape restoration in the Philippines: Implementation, motivations, challenges and future directions’, the researchers interviewed 22 key informants and held five focus group discussions involving stakeholders connected with ANR projects. Their findings show that natural regeneration can involve locating young trees, reducing grass competition, protecting recovering sites, and maintaining firebreaks.Three Philippine restoration projects used different approaches for forest recoveryThe study examined three ANR projects, that is, Carood, AFoCO, and NGP-ANR. Carood and AFoCO relied on naturally regenerating native woody species rather than enrichment planting. Workers located and marked regenerating trees, reduced competition from grasses through ring weeding, grass pressing, or manual pulling, and protected sites with firebreaks. These projects were established in areas affected by forest fires, livestock grazing, timber poaching, slash-and-burn agriculture, and wildlife hunting.NGP-ANR sites in Southern Leyte followed a different approach. They used high-density enrichment planting of native tree species in post-logging open forests. The researchers classified Carood and AFoCO as sustained projects because appropriate implementation and maintenance continued, while NGP-ANR was considered unsustained because maintenance was largely discontinued and practices deviated from ANR guidelines in practice.Why communities and organisations are adopting natural regenerationPeople involved in ANR projects were motivated by several economic, environmental, technical, and policy factors. Socioeconomic incentives were the strongest drivers, especially income and livelihood opportunities linked to project participation. Environmental motivations included biodiversity conservation, watershed protection, climate change mitigation, and disaster risk reduction.Community engagement, cultural values, capacity building, and institutional requirements also influenced participation. The study found that Carood and AFoCO participants were compensated according to the number of regenerants identified and managed per hectare. In Carood, people’s organizations could plant cash crops, fruit trees, and vegetables within firebreaks, creating an additional incentive. The projects also aimed to protect critical watersheds, demonstrate ANR, restore degraded forests, improve biodiversity and ecosystem services, and build local capacity through community involvement.Why long-term forest recovery remains difficult for ANR projectsMaintaining natural regeneration over time remains difficult. The researchers identified eight broad challenge areas that are funding and livelihood issues, environmental challenges, monitoring and sustainability concerns, community engagement, technical and logistical difficulties, political and institutional problems, local pressures and illegal activities, and land tenure and rights issues.Limited funding was the most pressing concern reported by many respondents. Forest fires were another major practical problem, particularly at Carood and AFoCO sites. The standard three-year project period was also considered insufficient for sustained regeneration.Better funding and protection are needed to sustain forest recoveryThe researchers identified several ways to strengthen ANR in the Philippines. Their recommendations include longer project timeframes, secure long-term funding, stronger site protection and maintenance, sustainable livelihood programmes, better technical capacity, stronger policy support and more secure land and tree tenure. Regular monitoring and impact assessments were also recommended to demonstrate the socio-ecological benefits of natural regeneration and encourage wider adoption.Protection measures included better firebreak design and maintenance, watchtowers, huts, and signs to improve surveillance. The study also highlights the importance of policy changes around native tree use, because harvesting restrictions can reduce the economic benefits communities receive from regenerating forests.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: It's three strikes and you're out for China. Trump should make this Xi's last chance
articles.summary: Xi Jinping arrives in Washington as a diminished leader facing military purges, Huawei turmoil, and a stumbling economy ahead of Trump talks.
articles.body: Expectations are low for breakthroughs when Xi Jinping meets President Donald Trump in Washington, D.C. this week. If China remains intransigent during the high-stakes diplomacy, it will be time for America to end decades of dialogue with Beijing. The Trump administration is setting the bar low for the summit. A continuation of last October’s trade truce, reached when the two leaders met in South Korea, is the most that officials are now hoping for. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been talking with a Chinese delegation about an extension. The truce expires November 10. XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT The Chinese should be happy with no disruption in the relationship. On Thursday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in the words of China’s Global Times, that "China-US relations have generally moved along the path toward a constructive relationship of strategic stability." Of course, China wants "stability." The Chinese side, in a stable environment, will be able to continue dangerous and unacceptable conduct, such as selling fentanyl, stealing U.S. intellectual property, engaging in predatory trade practices, supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine, maintaining secret police stations on American soil. And helping Iran kill American service personnel in the Persian Gulf. TRUMP SAYS CHINA 'SPIES' ON US AFTER REPORT TIES CHINESE IMAGERY TO IRAN STRIKE China has made its satellites available to that regime for targeting U.S. forces. On March 1, Iran almost certainly used that targeting data to kill six American service members in Kuwait. In July, Iran again relied upon Chinese satellite data to kill three more Americans, this time in Jordan. Washington’s China diplomacy has completely failed. TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS It is not hard to see why. American leaders have been pursuing dialogue with China since the early 1970s, when U.S. diplomats literally chased their Chinese counterparts to set up the summit in Beijing between President Nixon and Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong. America’s ardent desire to maintain dialogue has fed the already inflated sense of self-importance of Chinese leaders. Not surprisingly, this approach over the course of decades has coincided with — and almost certainly been the cause of — a marked deterioration in Chinese behavior. President Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi in May and made little discernible progress on contentious issues, so what more can be accomplished now? At some point, the United States needs to lose patience. For one thing, Xi Jinping’s arrogance at the May summit was stunning. On the first day of the event, he publicly mentioned the Thucydides Trap, a reference to a declining hegemon dangerously challenging a rising power. The insult was indirect, but nonetheless unmistakable. BEHIND SUMMIT SMILES, XI GIVES BLUNT WARNING TO TRUMP OF 'CLASHES' AND 'CONFLICTS' Even more insulting, the Chinese leader on the first day talked about the "new era," his phrase for the period in which the U.S. has been pushed to the sidelines and China dominates the world. As Charles Burton of the Sinopsis think tank noted, "Xi views himself as the modern heir of China’s lineage of great emperors, so the concept of fair and reciprocal relations with any foreign country is simply absent from his worldview." Today, Xi is still arrogant, but will arrive in the American capital a diminished figure. That gives Trump leverage, but, on the other hand, it reduces Xi’s room to maneuver. AMERICA HOLDS THE ADVANTAGE AS TRUMP MEETS XI IN HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT "President Trump may not fully appreciate, despite all the pomp and circumstance that he is offering, that he is engaging a Communist Party general secretary whose strength and authority domestically has been considerably weakened by a crisis of confidence in his leadership," said Burton, also a former Canadian diplomat in Beijing. Extraordinary events have been occurring in recent days at the top of the Communist Party. On Monday, the Communist Party announced the expulsion from the ruling organization of the country’s most senior uniformed officer, Gen. Zhang Youxia, and another general on the Central Military Commission, which controls the People’s Liberation Army. The pair was formally charged with corruption, disloyalty, and other serious disciplinary breaches. The charges suggest the generals had tried to seize power and depose Xi. NEWT GINGRICH: XI IS COMING TO WASHINGTON. HE SHOULD BRING ONE UNEXPECTED GUEST There is, at the same time, widespread domestic discontent over China’s stumbling economy and persistent questions about Xi’s health. If all this were not bad enough, Xi is coming off an unsuccessful BRICS summit in New Delhi, calling into question his handling of the country’s affairs. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION All this indicates that China’s leader cannot deal constructively with Trump this week. "Xi enters these talks as a beleaguered figure seeking to shore up his domestic position," Burton points out. "Fabricating friction with the West provides a convenient foreign distraction, allowing state media to divert public attention from internal instability and Xi’s faltering policy agendas." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In short, dialogue with China promises to be unproductive this week. If it is, we should stop talking and begin doing something effective.
